intro: The fourth group is where this treatise becomes, unmistakably, a practical meditation manual — food, sleep, posture, breath, and mind, worked through in the kind of hands-on detail a beginning practitioner could actually follow. This is likely the single most quoted and most practically useful passage in the whole work.

zh: 第四、調五法者：一者、調節飲食；二者、調節眠睡；三者、調身；四者、調氣息；五者、調心。所以者何？今借近譬以況斯法，如世陶師，欲造眾器，先須善巧調泥，令使不強不軟，然後可就輪繩。亦如彈琴，先應調絃，令寬急得所，方可入哢，出諸妙曲。行者修心亦復如是，善調五事，必使和適，則三昧易生；若有所不調，多諸妨難，善根難發。
en: Fourth, harmonizing the five things: first, regulating food and drink; second, regulating sleep; third, harmonizing the body; fourth, harmonizing the breath; fifth, harmonizing the mind. Why is this? Here, a familiar comparison may be borrowed to illustrate this method. It is like a potter who, wishing to fashion various vessels, must first skillfully knead the clay, making it neither too hard nor too soft, before it can be set upon the turning wheel and cord. It is also like tuning a lute: the strings must first be tuned, neither too slack nor too taut, before one can begin to play and produce every wondrous melody from it. The practitioner cultivating the mind is exactly the same: by skillfully harmonizing these five things, ensuring they are properly attuned, samādhi arises with ease; but if any of them is left unharmonized, many obstacles and difficulties arise, and wholesome roots are hard to bring forth.

zh: 第一、調食者，夫食之為法本，欲資身進道，食若過飽，則氣急身滿，百脈不通，令心閉塞，坐念不安。若食過少，則身羸心懸，意慮不固。此皆非得定之道。復次，若食穢濁之物，令人心識惛迷；若食不宜身物，則動宿疾，使四大違反。此為修定之初，深須慎之，故云身安則道隆。經云：「飯食知節量，常樂在閑處，心靜樂精進，是名諸佛教。」第二、調睡眠者，夫眠是無明惑覆之法，雖不可縱之，若都不眠，則心神虛恍；若其眠寐過多，非唯廢修聖法，亦復空喪功夫，令心暗晦，善根沈沒。當覺悟無常，調伏睡眠，令神道清白，念心明淨，如是乃可棲心聖境，三昧現前。故經云：「初夜、後夜亦勿有廢，無以睡眠因緣，令一生空過，無所得也。當念無常之火燒諸世間，早求自度，勿睡眠也。」
en: First, regulating food: as for food as a practice, its original purpose is to sustain the body in order to advance on the path. If one eats to excess, the breath becomes constricted and the body feels full, the hundred channels fail to circulate, the mind becomes stopped up, and sitting meditation is left unsettled. If one eats too little, the body grows weak and the mind restless, unable to settle its thoughts firmly. Neither of these is the way to attain concentration. Furthermore, if one eats impure and turbid things, the mind and consciousness become dull and confused; if one eats things unsuited to one's own constitution, dormant illnesses are stirred up and the four elements thrown into disorder. This is the very beginning of cultivating concentration, and must be attended to with the greatest care — hence it is said, "when the body is at ease, the path flourishes." As the sūtra says: "Eating with a knowledge of proper measure, constantly delighting in dwelling in a quiet place, with a still mind delighting in diligence — this is what every buddha has taught."

Second, regulating sleep: sleep is a dharma by which the delusion of ignorance covers over the mind; though it should not be indulged, if one does not sleep at all, the mind and spirit become empty and vacant; and if one sleeps to excess, this not only neglects the cultivation of the noble Dharma, but also wastes one's effort in vain, darkening and clouding the mind and causing wholesome roots to sink beneath the surface. One should awaken to impermanence and subdue sleep, so that the pathway of the spirit becomes pure and bright, and the mindful heart becomes clear and undefiled — only in this way can the mind come to dwell in the noble realm, with samādhi manifesting before it. Hence the sūtra says: "Do not neglect the first and last watches of the night either — do not let the cause and condition of sleep cause an entire life to pass by in vain, gaining nothing at all. One should be mindful that the fire of impermanence burns all the worlds, and swiftly seek one's own liberation, rather than sleeping."

items.en: Body, Breath, and Mind: Entering Meditation

zh: 第三、調身；第四、調息；第五、調心。此應合用，不得別說，但有初、中、後方法不同，是則入住出相有異。第一、入禪調三事者，行人欲入三昧，調身之宜，若在定外，行住進止，動靜運為，悉須詳審。若所作麁獷，則氣息隨麁。以氣麁故，則心散難錄。兼復坐時煩憒，心不恬怡，是以雖在定外，亦須用心逆作方便。後入禪時，須善安身得所。初至繩床，即前安坐處，每令安隱，久久無妨。次當正脚，若半跏坐，以左脚置右髀上，牽來近身，令左脚指與右髀齊，右脚指與左髀齊。若欲全跏，即上下右脚䟤置左脚上。次解寬衣帶周正，不令坐時脫落。次當安手，以左掌置右手上，重累手相對，頓置左脚上，牽近身，當心而安，正身，先當挺動其身，并諸支節，作七八反，如自按摩法，勿令手足差異。竟即正身端直，令脊相對，勿曲勿聳。次正頭頸，令鼻與臍相對，不偏不邪，不低不昂，平面正住。次開口吐胸中穢氣。吐法：開口放氣，自恣而出，想身分中百脈不通處，教悉隨氣而出盡；閉口，鼻中內清氣。如是至三。若身息調和，但一亦足。次當閉口，脣齒纔相拄著，舌向上齶。次當閉眼，纔令斷外光而已。當端身正坐，猶如奠石，無得身首四支竊爾搔動。是為初入禪定調身之法。舉要言之，不寬不急，是身調相。
en: Third, harmonizing the body; fourth, harmonizing the breath; fifth, harmonizing the mind. These three should be applied together, and cannot properly be explained separately — though the methods do differ across the beginning, middle, and end, corresponding to the different marks of entering, abiding in, and emerging from meditation.

First, entering dhyāna and harmonizing the three things — beginning with the body. When a practitioner wishes to enter samādhi, the harmonizing of the body should begin even before formal concentration: walking, standing, moving forward, and coming to rest, every motion and stillness of the body, must all be carried out with careful attention. If one's actions are coarse and unrefined, the breath will follow suit and become coarse; and because the breath is coarse, the mind becomes scattered and hard to gather in. Moreover, if one is agitated and disturbed at the time of sitting, the mind will not be calm and at ease — hence, even while still outside formal concentration, one must already apply the mind in anticipation, preparing the way with skillful means.

When one then actually enters dhyāna, the body must be skillfully settled into its proper place. Upon first reaching the meditation seat, at the place where one is to sit, one should always make it comfortable and secure, so that no difficulty arises even after a long time. Next, the legs should be properly arranged: in the half-lotus posture, place the left foot upon the right thigh, drawing it close to the body, so that the toes of the left foot align with the right thigh and the toes of the right foot align with the left thigh. If the full lotus posture is desired, then further draw the right foot up and place it upon the left foot as well. Next, loosen and properly adjust the belt of one's robe, so that it does not come loose while sitting. Next, the hands should be settled: place the left palm upon the right hand, one resting upon the other, facing each other, set upon the left foot, drawn close to the body, and settled directly before the heart. Straighten the body: first sway and stretch the body and every limb and joint, doing this seven or eight times, as in a self-massage, taking care that the hands and feet are not left out of alignment. Once this is done, straighten the body directly upright, so that the spine is properly aligned, neither bent nor thrust upward. Next, straighten the head and neck, so that the nose is aligned directly with the navel, neither tilted nor crooked, neither lowered nor raised, the face level and settled straight ahead. Next, open the mouth and exhale the impure air from within the chest. The method of exhaling: open the mouth and release the breath, letting it flow out freely, imagining that, at every place within the body where the hundred channels are obstructed, the breath carries this obstruction entirely out with it as it leaves; then close the mouth and draw pure air in through the nose. Do this up to three times; if the body and breath are already well harmonized, even a single time is sufficient. Next, the mouth should be closed, the lips and teeth lightly touching, the tongue resting against the upper palate. Next, the eyes should be closed, allowing only enough light to be shut out and no more. The body should then be held upright and sitting straight, as steady as a placed stone, with no stealthy shifting or scratching of the body, head, or any of the four limbs. This is the method of harmonizing the body upon first entering dhyāna-concentration. Taking the essential point: neither too slack nor too tense — this is the mark of a properly harmonized body.

zh: 第二、初入禪調息法者。息調凡有四相：一、風；二、喘；三、氣；四、息。前三為不調相，後一為調相。云何風相？坐時鼻中息出入覺有聲。云何喘相？坐時雖無聲，而出入結滯不通，是喘相。云何氣相？坐時雖無聲，亦不結滯，而出入不細，是名氣相。息相者，不聲、不結、不麁，出入綿綿，若存若亡，資神安隱，情抱悅豫，此是息相。守風則散，守喘則結，守氣則勞，守息則定。復次，坐時有風、氣等三相，是名不調，而用心者則為患也，心亦難定。若欲調之，當依三法：一者、下著安心；二者、寬身體；三者、想氣遍毛孔，出入通同無障。若細其心，令息微微然，息調則眾患不生，其心易定。是名行者初入定時調息方法。舉要言之，不澁不滑，是息調相。第三、初入定調心者。調心有二義：一者、調伏亂念，不令越逸；二者、當令沈浮寬急得所。何等為沈相？若坐時心中昏暗，無所記錄，頭好低垂，是為沈相。爾時當繫念鼻端，令心住在緣中，無令散意，此可治沈。何等為浮相？若坐時心神飄動，身亦不安，念在異緣，此是浮相。爾時宜安心向下係緣，制諸亂念，心則定住，此則心易安靜。舉要言之，不沈不浮，是心調相。問曰：心得有寬急相不？答曰：亦有此事。心急相者，由坐中撮心，用念望得，因此入定，是故氣上向，胸臆急痛。當寬放其心，想氣流下，患自差矣。若心寬相者，覺心志遊漫，身好萎蛇，或口涎流，或時暗晦，爾時應當歛身急念，令心住在緣中，身體相持，以此為治。心有澁滑之相，推之可知。是為初入定時調心方法。欲入定時，本是從麁入細，是以身既為麁，息居其中，心最為細，以善方便調麁就細，令心安靜，此則入定初方便也。
en: Second, the method of harmonizing the breath upon first entering dhyāna. The harmonizing of the breath has, in all, four marks: wind, panting, breath-with-effort, and true breath. The first three are unharmonized marks; the last alone is the harmonized mark. What is the mark of wind? While sitting, the breath going in and out through the nose is felt to make a sound. What is the mark of panting? While sitting, though there is no sound, the breath going in and out is obstructed and does not flow smoothly — this is the mark of panting. What is the mark of breath-with-effort? While sitting, though there is no sound and no obstruction, the breath going in and out is not fine and subtle — this is called the mark of breath-with-effort. As for the mark of true breath: no sound, no obstruction, no coarseness, going in and out continuously and finely, as though it were present yet almost imperceptible, sustaining the spirit at ease, the feelings held in quiet contentment — this is the mark of true breath. Dwelling on wind leads to scatteredness; dwelling on panting leads to obstruction; dwelling on breath-with-effort leads to fatigue; dwelling on true breath leads to concentration.

Furthermore, while sitting, if the marks of wind, panting, or breath-with-effort are present, this is called unharmonized, and applying the mind while in this state becomes itself a source of trouble, making the mind hard to concentrate. To harmonize it, one should rely on three methods: first, settling the mind low and at ease; second, loosening and relaxing the body; third, imagining the breath pervading every pore, going in and out uniformly and without obstruction. If the mind is made fine and subtle in this way, the breath will naturally become faint and gentle; once the breath is harmonized, every trouble ceases to arise, and the mind concentrates with ease. This is the method of harmonizing the breath for a practitioner first entering concentration. Taking the essential point: neither rough nor slippery — this is the mark of a properly harmonized breath.

Third, harmonizing the mind upon first entering concentration. Harmonizing the mind has two aspects: first, subduing scattered thoughts, not allowing the mind to run wild and escape; second, ensuring that sinking and floating, slackness and tension, are each brought to their proper measure. What is the mark of sinking? If, while sitting, the mind is dark and dull, retaining nothing, the head inclined to droop — this is the mark of sinking. At such a time, one should fix the mind at the tip of the nose, holding it steady upon this object, not allowing the intention to scatter — this can remedy sinking. What is the mark of floating? If, while sitting, the mind and spirit drift and stir restlessly, the body also unsettled, thoughts wandering off to other objects — this is the mark of floating. At such a time, one should settle the mind, directing it downward and fixing it upon its object, restraining every scattered thought, and the mind will then come to rest in concentration — in this way the mind is easily made calm and still. Taking the essential point: neither sinking nor floating — this is the mark of a properly harmonized mind.

Question: Can the mind also have marks of slackness and tension? Answer: This too occurs. The mark of a tense mind arises from gathering the mind too forcefully during sitting, applying thought in eager anticipation of results; because of this, when entering concentration, the breath rises upward and the chest feels tight and pained. One should loosen and relax the mind, imagining the breath flowing downward, and the trouble will naturally subside. As for the mark of a slack mind: one becomes aware that the mind's intent has grown loose and wandering, the body inclined to slump and sag, perhaps drooling from the mouth, or at times growing dull and clouded; at such a time, one should draw the body in and apply thought more firmly, holding the mind steady upon its object and the body held firmly together — this is the remedy. The mind may also have marks of roughness or slipperiness, which can be understood by the same reasoning. This is the method of harmonizing the mind upon first entering concentration.

When one wishes to enter concentration, the movement is, by its very nature, from the coarse into the fine: the body, being coarsest, comes first; the breath, situated between, comes next; the mind, being finest of all, comes last. By skillful means, harmonizing the coarse until it becomes fine, the mind is settled and stilled — this is the initial expedient means for entering concentration.

This is the treatise's fullest, most concrete instruction so far — full-lotus and half-lotus posture, the specific sequence of settling hands and spine, the four grades of breath from audible "wind" down to true, imperceptible breath, and a genuinely practical taxonomy of what can go wrong with the meditating mind (sinking versus floating, tense versus slack) paired with a specific remedy for each. The overall logic — body first, then breath, then mind, moving from coarse to fine — recurs as the organizing principle for the rest of this section: the same three things, and the same coarse-to-fine movement, are worked through again for abiding in meditation and for emerging from it.

quiz.q: Which two similes explain why the five things must be harmonized?
options: a potter kneading clay neither too hard nor too soft; tuning a lute neither too slack nor too taut
washing cloth; soap-pod lye
a well-trained horse; a spring in rock
drilling for fire; repaying a debt
quiz.why: "It is like a potter who ... must first skillfully knead the clay, making it neither too hard nor too soft ... It is also like tuning a lute: the strings must first be tuned, neither too slack nor too taut." The well-trained horse appears in the verse on emerging from meditation.

quiz.q: What does the text say happens if one eats to excess?
options: the breath is constricted, the body full, the channels blocked, the mind stopped up, and sitting unsettled
old illnesses stir and the elements are disordered
the body weak, the mind restless
the mind becomes dull and confused
quiz.why: "If one eats to excess, the breath becomes constricted and the body feels full, the hundred channels fail to circulate, the mind becomes stopped up, and sitting meditation is left unsettled." Weakness comes from eating too little, dullness from impure food, and stirring old illness from unsuitable food.

quiz.q: When entering dhyāna, how is the half-lotus posture arranged?
options: place the right foot on the left thigh
both feet crossed beneath the knees
place the left foot on the right thigh, drawn close, so the left toes align with the right thigh and the right toes with the left thigh
both feet on the ground
quiz.why: "In the half-lotus posture, place the left foot upon the right thigh, drawing it close to the body, so that the toes of the left foot align with the right thigh and the toes of the right foot align with the left thigh." For full lotus the right foot is then placed upon the left.

quiz.q: Of the four marks of breath, which one is the harmonized mark?
options: panting: obstructed
wind: audible
true breath: no sound, no obstruction, not coarse, continuous and fine, as though present yet almost imperceptible
breath-with-effort: silent and smooth but not fine
quiz.why: "The harmonizing of the breath has, in all, four marks: wind, panting, breath-with-effort, and true breath. The first three are unharmonized marks; the last alone is the harmonized mark ... no sound, no obstruction, no coarseness, going in and out continuously and finely, as though it were present yet almost imperceptible."

quiz.q: "Dwelling on wind leads to scatteredness, on panting to obstruction, on breath-with-effort to fatigue" — and dwelling on true breath?
options: leads to sleep
leads to scatteredness
leads to heat
leads to concentration
quiz.why: "Dwelling on wind leads to scatteredness; dwelling on panting leads to obstruction; dwelling on breath-with-effort leads to fatigue; dwelling on true breath leads to concentration." When unharmonized, settle the mind low, relax the body, and imagine the breath pervading the pores.

quiz.q: If, while sitting, the mind is dark and dull and the head droops, what mark is this, and what is the remedy?
options: slackness; draw in the body and apply thought firmly
tension; relax and imagine the breath flowing down
sinking; fix the mind at the tip of the nose, holding it on the object
floating; settle the mind downward on its object
quiz.why: "If, while sitting, the mind is dark and dull, retaining nothing, the head inclined to droop — this is the mark of sinking. At such a time, one should fix the mind at the tip of the nose." Floating is remedied by settling the mind downward, tension by relaxing, and slackness by drawing in.
